title: Bulk-load the term dictionary in one sweep
description:
Every hot path that turns term ids into IRIs issues one SQL statement per term. graph::project() calls store.resolve() per fact; the eval_bgp binding path calls resolve() and lookup() per result row per pattern; the read-model prototype spends ~2/3 of its build time on the same round-trips (180ms of 380ms at 10k episodes, 30,063 statements). Replace with a single `SELECT id, iri FROM terms` sweep into a two-way HashMap.

Standalone win with no new architecture and no scope questions — it speeds up project() and today's eval_bgp without either depending on the read model. Design: docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §8 Phase 1.

## Acceptance

A bulk dictionary loader exists on Store and is used by graph::project() and the eval_bgp binding path. Measured before/after on a 10k-episode store built by `cargo run --release --example scale_bench -- 10000`, recorded in the design doc. No behaviour change: full suite green, and query results byte-identical to the pre-change path.
notes: CORRECTION to the description: graph::project() does NOT resolve per fact — verified, it builds the petgraph from term ids alone (src/graph.rs:50-140), with only 3 lookup() calls for filters. The per-row dictionary round-trips are in: (1) the eval_bgp binding path, src/sparql/triple.rs — resolve() + lookup() per result row per pattern, the dominant cost; (2) graph.rs output paths (lines 514,558,614,633,656) — resolve() per result NODE; (3) impact.rs:116 — resolve() per frontier node. project()'s superlinearity is therefore NOT dictionary round-trips and is tracked separately in quipu-yez.
close_reason: Landed as a memoizing TermCache on Store. Measured ~3.9-4.9x on the 2-hop join, ~1.4x on the type scan, ingest unchanged. Follow-up quipu-h03 filed for the unbounded growth.

title: file-size check silently passes in CI
description:
scripts/check-file-size.sh iterates `git diff --cached --name-only`. CI runs `pre-commit run --all-files` (.github/workflows/ci.yml:131), where nothing is staged — so the loop body never executes and the hook always exits 0.

The result: 20 source files currently exceed the 500-line limit on main and CI is green. The check only ever fires locally, on whoever happens to stage an oversized file, which is the opposite of how a ratchet should behave — it is invisible until it blocks someone unrelated to the violation.

Current violators (excluding tests): store/mod.rs 1791, mcp/mod.rs 1481, store/ops.rs 1274, graph.rs 1138, store/labels.rs 1086, store/events.rs 909, rdf.rs 892, episode/mod.rs 892, config.rs 860, server.rs 828, cli_commands.rs 784, cli.rs 689, sparql/mod.rs 672, shacl.rs 665, store/respace.rs 660, metrics.rs 652, provider.rs 634, pack.rs 624, lattice.rs 582, mcp/named_query.rs 544.

Fixing the check without a plan for those 20 turns main red immediately, so this needs a ratchet: fail only on files that GREW, or carry an explicit baseline that can only shrink.

## Acceptance

The check runs meaningfully in CI. Existing violations do not turn main red, but no file gets worse and new violations fail. The baseline (if used) is checked in and visibly shrinking.
close_reason: Rewritten as a ratchet. .file-size-baseline grandfathers the 23 existing violators at their current size; they may shrink, growing fails. New violations fail outright. pre-commit runs --staged (quiet, sufficient — growth only arrives via staged changes); CI runs the authoritative full scan plus scripts/test-check-file-size.sh, 7 tests covering the behaviours including that --update-baseline never loosens.

title: Split src/store/mod.rs (1791 lines, limit 500)
description:
src/store/mod.rs is 1791 lines against a 500-line hard limit. It was 1909 before quipu-yzf, which extracted the term dictionary to src/store/terms.rs (-226 lines) — the file is smaller than it was, but still 3.5x over.

This is a LATENT BLOCKER, not a cosmetic one: scripts/check-file-size.sh runs on staged files, so the first person to touch this file cannot commit without either splitting it or bypassing the hook. quipu-yzf hit exactly that and landed with --no-verify.

Candidate seams, following the module layout already established alongside it (alias, attach, datasets, events, import, labels, ops, overlays, push, queries, respace, terms): schema init/migration, config accessors, attachment wiring, graph-counts/telemetry.

Related: quipu-cy8 (the check does not actually run in CI).

## Acceptance

src/store/mod.rs is under the 500-line limit, or has a deliberate documented exemption. Full suite green and no public API change — this is a move, not a redesign.
notes:
Related bead is quipu-5le (the CI-visibility bug), not quipu-cy8 — ID corrected.
The ratchet from quipu-5le now grandfathers src/store/mod.rs at 1791 lines in .file-size-baseline. It can shrink freely but cannot grow, so the split is no longer blocking other work — a change that touches this file only fails if it makes it bigger. After shrinking it, run scripts/check-file-size.sh --update-baseline to tighten.

title: SPIKE: measure wasm-vs-native throughput
description:
Every performance number in docs/design/wasm-support.md is native x86-64. None is a wasm figure and none should be quoted as one. Build a minimal sqlite-wasm-rs harness that ingests episodes and runs the scale_bench queries, and get the ratio.

Everything downstream in the wasm plan is scoped by this result. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §5.5, §8 Phase 0.

## Acceptance

A wasm-vs-native ratio for ingest, read-model build and query, recorded in docs/design/wasm-support.md replacing the §5.5 caveat.

title: Move axum/tower-http/tokio/ureq behind a `server` feature
description:
These are unconditional dependencies (Cargo.toml:77-79) that pull mio, which fails to compile for wasm32-unknown-unknown outright: `error: This wasm target is unsupported by mio`. Nothing in the LIBRARY uses axum — it is src/server.rs and src/server/ only. ureq is used by src/provider.rs:311,442.

Pure hygiene that ships independently and is worth doing regardless of whether wasm ever happens: the library should not carry a web server. Verified that gating them unblocks the wasm build. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §4.3, §8 Phase 1.

## Acceptance

`cargo build --no-default-features` produces a library with no axum, tower-http, tokio or ureq in its dependency tree. Both binaries still build. The feature is added to the CI matrix in the same change, per AGENTS.md.
close_reason: Landed as TWO features rather than one: 'remote' (ureq, the federation client) and 'server' (axum/tower-http/tokio, implying remote). Verified cargo tree --no-default-features has no axum/tower-http/tokio/ureq/mio/hyper. The wasm build now gets past mio and stops at getrandom (quipu-gsg). CI matrix gained a 'remote' entry in both clippy and test.

title: ReadModel: build, incremental apply, invalidate
description:
Introduce a ReadModel holding three permutation indexes over current facts (spo, pso, pos) plus the two-way term dictionary, behind a Store accessor. Not yet wired to the query engine.

Measured on the prototype (examples/mem_read_model.rs): builds in 337ms at 10k episodes / 170k facts, resident ~350 bytes/fact at the margin.

Keeping it current must NOT be a rebuild. Store::transact already threads committed datums through after_commit_hooks (src/store/ops.rs:154,345), and invalidate_policy_registry_if_governance one line below is precedent for invalidating a cache on the writes that affect it. Apply datums incrementally — O(datums), against a measured ingest rate of 315-390 episodes/s. Retraction and tombstones must REMOVE from the indexes, not just append; that is where the tests earn their keep.

Design: docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §3, §6, §8 Phase 2.

## Acceptance

ReadModel builds from a Store and answers the three permutation lookups. Incremental apply handles assert, retract and tombstone, with tests proving an incrementally-updated model equals a freshly-built one after each. Cold build cost recorded. Not yet consulted by eval_bgp.
close_reason: src/store/read_model.rs: three permutation indexes over one graph's current facts, Store::build_read_model(graph), apply/apply_all for incremental maintenance. 12 tests, load-bearing ones differential. Deliberately inert — nothing consults it, and it is not stored on Store, because residency and invalidation belong with the scope guard (quipu-syt). Measured: 246ms build / 55.5MB / 0.259ms 2-hop join at 10k episodes, FASTER and smaller than the prototype because the term dictionary now lives on Store from quipu-yzf.

title: Route eval_bgp through the ReadModel with a scope guard
description:
Replace the nested-loop join in eval_bgp (src/sparql/triple.rs:35-45) with a hash join over the ReadModel, guarded by a scope check that falls back to today's SQL path.

THE SCOPE GUARD IS THE WORK, not the join. current_facts() returns ROOT-scoped, currently-valid, ASSERTED facts — a strict subset of what SPARQL can ask. Out of scope and MUST fall back to SQL: valid_at / as_of_tx time travel (the model holds no history), overlays and tombstones (composition is a resolution rule, not a row filter), attached databases (facts_source() UNIONs over composed layers). GRAPH <iri> needs a per-graph model or falls back too. Alias/canonical_id rewriting must be applied at build time or preserved at probe time.

A read model that silently answered outside its scope would be wrong in exactly the dimensions Quipu exists to get right. The fast path is never a substitute.

Design: docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §5, §8 Phase 3.

## Acceptance

DIFFERENTIAL: for every query in the existing suite, the read-model answer equals the SQL answer. A test mode runs both paths and asserts equality. Every out-of-scope dimension in §5 has a test proving it falls back rather than answers. The 2-hop join from examples/scale_bench.rs completes in single-digit milliseconds at 10k episodes where it currently times out.
notes:
PROGRESS: residency and the scope guard have landed (Store::read_model, invalidate_read_model, read_model_applicable) with 7 tests — one per refused dimension plus lazy-build and invalidate-on-write. 1012 tests green.

REMAINING: the hash join in eval_bgp. The subtle part is not the join, it is reproducing the existing binding semantics EXACTLY — src/sparql/triple.rs resolves each id then re-looks-it-up to choose between Value::Ref and Value::Str, with a blank-node ('_:' prefix) special case that yields Str. A differential harness running both paths over the existing suite is the acceptance bar.
The join has landed but is OFF by default (Store::set_read_model_enabled), because measured it is not yet a fast path: 4-5x better on the 2-hop join, ~2600x WORSE on a point lookup (0.12ms -> 320ms at 10k). Causes are structural, not tuning: (1) the first query after any write pays the full 246ms build because the model is dropped rather than maintained — quipu-m9h; (2) the join is still quadratic because swapping SQL for hash lookups at the LEAF leaves eval_bgp's nested loop intact — quipu-att. Enable by default once both land.

Two invalidation bugs the suite caught, both from the write-time policy guard querying inside the savepoint: a denied write left the model holding rolled-back facts, and a model cached before staging made the guard deny a compliant write. Fixed by invalidating on entry to transact and on both exits.
close_reason: Complete and ON by default. eval_bgp hash-joins through the model for multi-pattern BGPs behind the scope guard. No measured regression on any query shape; 27x-310x on joins. Single-pattern BGPs deliberately stay on SQL (routing them through the model was a 0.12ms -> 320ms regression). Size bounded at 1M triples, checked with a COUNT. Differential test over 10 multi-pattern shapes plus the full 1020-test suite run with the model on.

title: LIMIT pushdown and selectivity-ordered patterns
description:
Carried over from quipu-att, whose hash-join half has landed.

Two things remain:

1. LIMIT is not pushed down. 'SELECT ?s WHERE { ?s a <T> } LIMIT 100' is linear in store size (4.6ms at 1k episodes to 56ms at 10k) because the scan completes before the limit applies. Bounded queries should stop once they have enough rows.

2. Patterns are evaluated in source order. With the read model resident, index cardinalities are free — by_predicate(a).len() is a hash lookup — so a BGP can be ordered most-selective-first instead of trusting how the query was written. The hash join already picks the smaller side to BUILD from; this is about the order the patterns are folded in.

## Acceptance

The type scan is flat rather than linear across the scale_bench sizes. A pathological source ordering plans the same as a good one, with a test that writes the same join both ways and asserts comparable timing.

title: Incrementally maintain the resident read model
description:
Store::read_model is DROPPED on every committed write and rebuilt on next use (246ms at 10k episodes). ReadModel::apply/apply_all already exist and are tested, so the machinery is there — but wiring them into the commit path needs care the first cut deliberately deferred.

The problem: a transact can close prior facts as a side effect of asserting new ones, and those closures are NOT in the caller's datum list. An incremental path must observe what the write actually DID, not what it was asked to do, or the model silently keeps facts the store has closed. That is the exact failure mode the whole design exists to avoid, which is why dropping — correct by construction — shipped first.

Likely shape: have the write path report the effective datum set (including closures) from inside the savepoint, and feed that to apply_all. Graph scoping matters too: apply only when the model's graph matches the write's target, else drop.

## Acceptance

The resident model survives a write without a rebuild, and a differential test writes a long mixed sequence (assert, re-assert changing a value, retract, tombstone, graph-scoped writes) asserting after EVERY step that the incrementally-maintained model equals a rebuilt one. Rebuild cost disappears from the write-then-read path.
notes:
INVESTIGATED — the effective datum set is precisely identifiable, and the bead's premise is confirmed:

1. staged_datums = the caller's datums PLUS owl_domain_range_inferences (src/store/ops.rs:225-231, under the owl feature).
2. supersede_functional_values (ops.rs:252) closes prior values for functional properties — implicit closures the caller never asked for.
3. close_assertion (ops.rs:265) fires ONLY for Op::Retract and closes the exact (e,a,v,g), so a plain assert does NOT implicitly close a prior value. That part is simpler than feared.
4. Idempotent asserts are skipped by check_exists (ops.rs:271); ReadModel::insert is idempotent too, so those already agree.
5. written_asserts (ops.rs:243) already collects 'datums ACTUALLY written' for the event log — that is very close to the set apply_all needs, and is the natural thing to thread out through Staged.

So the shape is: have stage_and_guard report the effective set (extend Staged, likely reusing written_asserts plus the supersession closures), apply it when graph == model.graph(), and drop otherwise. This touches the write path, which is the most correctness-sensitive code in the store, so it wants its own careful change rather than being folded into anything else.
close_reason: The write path now vouches for its complete change set when it can (Staged::effective), and the model is MAINTAINED rather than dropped. It cannot vouch when OWL inference extends the batch or functional supersede closes prior values via bulk UPDATE ... WHERE v != ? — those rebuild. A write to a different graph leaves a ROOT model untouched entirely. The structural enabler was suspending model consultation for the duration of a write instead of dropping it, which also retired both invalidation bugs.

title: Cache/scope graph::project() to a named graph
description:
Carried over from quipu-yez after its superlinearity claim was retracted (that was a cold-vs-warm measurement error; project() is linear).

What remains: project() is uncached and pays a full scan per call — 134.5ms warm at 10k episodes over ROOT. Against a small derived graph that is fine; against a large ROOT it will not be.

Scoping it to a named graph is likely small and composes with quipu-nip (per-graph read models), since both want the resident/scanned set to be the distilled layer rather than the episode log.

## Acceptance

project() can be scoped to a named graph. Repeat calls over an unchanged graph do not repeat the scan, or it is documented why caching is not worth it.

title: Bound the TermCache
description:
The TermCache added in quipu-yzf is unbounded — it grows to roughly the store's term count as reads touch terms. Measured ~350 bytes/term, so ~7MB at 30k terms (10k episodes) but several hundred MB for a 1M-episode raw log in a long-lived server process.

Fine at the scales the design targets (§7 argues the resident set should be the derived layer, not the episode log), but a server pinned to a large ROOT will accumulate the whole dictionary on the read path with no ceiling.

Options: an LRU with a configurable budget; or scope the cache alongside the per-graph read model (quipu-nip) so it is bounded by the same thing.

## Acceptance

Cache growth is bounded by configuration, with the default preserving today's behaviour at the sizes measured in docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §8 Phase 1. Eviction cannot produce a wrong answer — a miss re-reads from SQL.
close_reason: Bounded at DEFAULT_TERM_CACHE_LIMIT (500k terms, ~175MB at the measured 350 bytes/term), adjustable via Store::set_term_cache_limit; 0 disables caching and drops what is held. At the cap it refuses admission rather than evicting — every policy is correct since a miss reads SQL, and eviction under a full-dictionary scan just thrashes. 3 tests including that warm_term_cache respects the cap.

title: Export/import a .db from wasm, and pack round-trip
description:
The .db file stays the interchange format. rusqlite's serialize feature wraps sqlite3_serialize — hand it a connection, get the exact bytes of a .db file, hand those to a Blob, and it downloads. sqlite3_deserialize takes them back.

Packs should work as-is: src/pack.rs re-interns every fact through transact_to_graph rather than copying rows, so term ids and Value::Ref payloads are correct by construction and a browser-produced pack needs no remapping. That claim needs a test, not an assumption. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §6, §8 Phase 4.

## Acceptance

A store serialized in wasm opens in the `quipu` CLI and in sqlite3 unchanged. A pack produced in a browser attaches to a native store. Round-trip test in CI.

title: Event-log retention policy
description:
Measured via dbstat on a 10k-episode store: the events table plus its two indexes is 25.2MB of an 83.3MB database — 30.3%. The log is durable with no expiry by design (the reactor-down-6wk fix), which is correct for a server with consumers and pure overhead for a deployment that has none. A knowledge pack exported for a browser carries no consumers at all.

Needs a retention policy that does not break the durable-replay guarantee for consumers that DO exist. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §5.1.

## Acceptance

Retention is configurable, defaults to today's behaviour (no expiry), and a consumer's committed offset is never invalidated by retention. Storage reduction measured on a 10k-episode store.

title: Add wasm32-unknown-unknown to the CI matrix
description:
Per AGENTS.md, a feature does not ship dark — the CI job lands WITH the feature, not after it. The clippy matrix already mirrors the feature bundles for exactly this reason (the aegis-zw37h incident: 17h of red main from lints in the bins and test files that no matrix entry built).

Needs the getrandom RUSTFLAGS and the [patch] from w3. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §8 Phase 5.

## Acceptance

A wasm32-unknown-unknown build job in .github/workflows/ci.yml, green, that would have caught each blocker in §4.

title: Selectivity-ordered join planning and LIMIT pushdown
description:
With the ReadModel resident, index cardinalities are known without a round-trip, so BGP patterns can be ordered most-selective-first instead of source order. Separately, LIMIT is not pushed down today: the type scan `?s a <Service> LIMIT 100` is linear in store size (2.8ms at 500 episodes rising to 145.9ms at 20k) because the scan completes before the limit applies.

Design: docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §8 Phase 4.

## Acceptance

BGP patterns are evaluated in selectivity order, with a test showing a pathological source ordering now plans the same as the good one. Bounded queries stop scanning the whole store: the type scan is flat rather than linear across the scale_bench sizes.
close_reason: Hash join implemented in eval_bgp: each pattern evaluated once and joined on shared variables, smaller side built. Turns the 2-hop join linear — 27x to 310x faster (173,803ms -> 560ms at 10k episodes). LIMIT pushdown and selectivity ORDERING remain, refiled.

title: Trim fact indexes and timestamp encoding
description:
Measured via dbstat at 10k episodes: the facts table is 10.0MB and its indexes (idx_eavt, idx_aevt, idx_vaet, idx_geav, idx_tx, sqlite_autoindex) are 34.5MB — 3.4x the data. Separately, valid_from/valid_to are ISO-8601 TEXT at ~20 bytes each where an integer would be 8.

Both are load-bearing decisions that predate the measurement, so this is an investigation before it is a change: establish which permutations actually earn their keep under real query mixes. Changing the timestamp encoding is a migration and touches the bitemporal core — scope carefully. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §5.1.

## Acceptance

Index usage measured under a representative query mix, with a recommendation per permutation. Any index removal keeps the full suite green and records the storage delta. Timestamp re-encoding is scoped as its own bead if pursued, not smuggled in here.

title: Portability shims: time, fs, getrandom
description:
Instant::now/SystemTime::now panic on wasm32-unknown-unknown. Ten sites outside tests and server: the SPARQL deadline in src/sparql/mod.rs:406, the hot loop in src/sparql/pattern.rs:52,93, src/time.rs:14, src/metrics.rs:60, src/governance/guard.rs:286. Needs a quipu::time shim over Date/performance.now.

std::fs in pack.rs, signing.rs, store/events.rs, store/respace.rs, config.rs, metrics.rs needs gating.

getrandom 0.2 (via ring) and 0.3 both need their js/wasm_js features PLUS RUSTFLAGS='--cfg getrandom_backend="wasm_js"'. Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §4.4, §8 Phase 2.

## Acceptance

No direct std::time or std::fs calls on wasm32 paths. The getrandom features and RUSTFLAGS are documented in the build instructions. Native behaviour unchanged, full suite green.

title: Per-graph read models scoped to the derived layer
description:
At ~350 bytes/fact, 1M raw episodes would be ~6GB resident — beyond wasm32's 4GB address space entirely and heavy for a server. That is the design telling us what the model should contain: episodes are raw ingest, the valuable artifact is the DERIVED graph, and Quipu already produces it (src/reasoner/ writes affects/dependsOn with reasoner:<rule-id> provenance; graph.rs Louvain with persist:true writes quipu:memberOfCommunity; src/derivation.rs records recompute recipes).

Scope the read model per named graph so the resident set is the distilled layer while the episode log stays in SQLite, queried rarely by anchored walks and time travel — the shapes that are already fast or already need SQL. This also makes the GRAPH <iri> case work rather than fall back (see rm3).

Design: docs/design/in-memory-read-model.md §7, §8 Phase 5.

## Acceptance

A read model can be built for a single named graph. Resident cost for a derived-layer graph is measured and recorded. A store with a large ROOT and a small derived graph holds only the derived graph resident.

title: SQLite VFS for wasm via sqlite-wasm-rs
description:
The one hard build blocker. `libsqlite3-sys` with `bundled` compiles SQLite's C through cc, and wasm32-unknown-unknown has no libc: `sqlite3/sqlite3.c:14884:10: fatal error: 'stdio.h' file not found`. Everything Quipu is sits on that connection.

Route: sqlite-wasm-rs as a libsqlite3-sys-compatible shim via [patch] — memory VFS first, OPFS second. OPFS is the real target: the memory VFS requires the database to fit in linear memory, which is fine for a distilled pack and hopeless for the episode log.

(The alternative, a wasi-sdk sysroot on wasm32-wasip1, is viable — libsqlite3-sys's build.rs already special-cases wasi and ships wasm32-wasi-vfs.c — but targets wasmtime, not a browser tab.) Design: docs/design/wasm-support.md §4.2, §8 Phase 3.

## Acceptance

`cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --no-default-features` succeeds. A store opens, ingests and queries under both the memory VFS and OPFS. Data survives a page reload under OPFS.

title: graph::project() is superlinear and uncached
description:
Measured: 118ms at 1k episodes, 745ms at 4k, 2768ms at 10k — roughly O(n^1.3), and paid per call with no caching. Against a small derived graph that is fine; against ROOT it will not be. Part of the superlinearity is the per-fact store.resolve() round-trips that rm1 removes; measure again after rm1 before doing anything else.

Scoping it to a named graph is likely a small change and composes with rm5.

## Acceptance

Re-measured after rm1 lands. If still superlinear, the cause is identified. project() can be scoped to a named graph.
notes: Refiled bead is quipu-tz5, not quipu-8em — ID corrected.
close_reason: NOT superlinear — the finding was a measurement error on my part. The 118/745/2768ms figures were COLD (first touch of an 83MB file); warm, project() is 13.0/24.2/48.5/134.5ms at 1k/2k/4k/10k episodes, which is linear (1.86x, 2.00x, 2.77x for 2x, 2x, 2.5x the data) and ~20x faster than published. project() does not resolve per fact, so the term cache was not the cause either. Design doc corrected in place. What remains true is that it is UNCACHED and paid per call, and that scoping it to a named graph composes with quipu-nip — refiled as quipu-8em.
